issues.title: Morocco backs Riyadh, calls for sanctions over Houthi attacks
issues.title_en: Morocco backs Riyadh, calls for sanctions over Houthi attacks
issues.summary: Morocco backs Riyadh, calls for sanctions over Houthi attacks The intervention came as Saudi Arabia faced a renewed barrage of attacks, including missiles and drones directed towards Riyadh and Khamis Mushait on September 26. Sunday 27/09/2026 Morocco’s King Mohammed VI chairs a meeting at the Royal Palace in Rabat, September 14, 2023. RABAT Morocco has thrown its support behind Saudi Arabia as a wave of Houthi missile and drone attacks raises wider regional concerns, with King Mohammed VI saying any assault on the kingdom amounts to an attack on Morocco and calling for international sanctions against those responsible. The intervention came as Saudi Arabia faced a renewed barrage of attacks, including missiles and drones directed towards Riyadh and Khamis Mushait on September 26. Saudi authorities said two ballistic missiles and two drones had been intercepted, with the missiles heading towards Khamis Mushait and the drones towards the capital. In messages to Saudi King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, King Mohammed VI said Morocco regarded the security of Saudi Arabia and the wider Gulf as directly linked to its own national security. “Any attack on Saudi Arabia is an attack on Morocco,” the monarch said, describing the defence of Saudi and Gulf interests as part of Morocco’s “shared strategic interests”. The unusually direct formulation underlined the depth of the political and strategic relationship between Rabat and Riyadh at a time when attacks originating from Yemen are increasingly affecting the security calculations of Gulf states. The Moroccan king expressed “deep concern and preoccupation” over attacks targeting civilian and economic facilities, vital infrastructure, cities and residential areas, while warning that the consequences extended beyond Saudi territory to the stability of the wider region. Particular emphasis was placed on Makkah and Medina, after Saudi authorities reported an intercepted drone near Makkah earlier in September. Saudi Arabia said on September 15 that its air defences destroyed a drone launched towards the holy city before it entered restricted airspace. For Rabat, the threat to the two holy cities gives the escalation a significance extending beyond conventional regional security concerns. King Mohammed VI said attempts to target the Islamic holy sites represented an assault not only on Saudi Arabia and those visiting the country, but on Muslims worldwide. “These despicable attacks and desperate attempts to undermine the security, stability and prosperity of the proud Saudi people do not represent only an attack on brotherly Saudi Arabia, its people, and those performing Umrah there,” he said. “They are a blatant attack on the feelings of more than one billion and 800 million Muslims across the world.” He condemned what he called “criminal acts” and held the Houthis and those supporting, financing or arming them responsible, calling for accountability under international law and the imposition of international sanctions. The Moroccan monarch also linked the escalation to United Nations resolutions dealing with Yemen and Red Sea security, citing Security Council Resolution 2216 of 2015 and Resolution 2722 of 2024. His reference to Resolution 2722 was particularly significant in the context of the wider security implications of the Houthi campaign. The resolution called for an immediate end to attacks on merchant and commercial vessels in the Red Sea, placing the protection of maritime traffic at the centre of the international response. Morocco’s message argued that the threat was therefore not confined to Saudi territory. Attacks on the kingdom’s cities and infrastructure are unfolding alongside wider disruption to maritime routes and energy flows, raising concerns about the potential economic consequences of an expanding regional conflict. The Houthi campaign has already included attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure. A September strike caused fires at a pumping station along the kingdom’s East-West pipeline, while other attacks have targeted Saudi cities and strategic facilities. The escalation has also triggered a broader effort to coordinate support for Riyadh. Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, Pakistan and Egypt said in a joint statement on September 22 that Saudi Arabia had the right to defend itself under international law and stressed the importance of safe navigation in the region. The ministers also called for dialogue and diplomacy as the sustainable route towards resolving regional conflicts. Three days later, the military chiefs of Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan met in Riyadh to discuss the threats facing the kingdom and begin putting their joint defence commitments into effect. The three countries’ Makkah Joint Defence Agreement provides that an armed attack against one party is considered an attack against all three. The sequence marks a widening of the response from political condemnation towards greater security coordination, as Riyadh faces attacks on several fronts. The Moroccan position adds another layer to that regional mobilisation. Rather than treating the Houthi attacks as a dispute limited to Yemen and Saudi Arabia, Rabat has framed them as a broader challenge to Arab security, state sovereignty, religious sites and international maritime security. That framing also reflects Morocco’s longstanding emphasis on its strategic ties with the Gulf. By describing Saudi and Gulf security as inseparable from Morocco’s own security, King Mohammed VI placed the kingdom’s confrontation with the Houthis within a wider conception of shared regional interests. The monarch warned that armed groups and the regional forces supporting them were pursuing policies that threatened neighbouring states, undermined stability and placed vital maritime corridors at risk. He said Morocco stood alongside Saudi Arabia in confronting those threats and called for a united position in defence of sovereignty, security and religious sanctities. The latest Houthi attacks have meanwhile continued to draw wider Arab condemnation. The Arab Interior Ministers Council condemned the September 26 missile and drone launches towards Riyadh and Khamis Mushait, saying attacks on civilian and civilian infrastructure threatened regional security and stability.
